why: The Greek plus (and its repeated 'not so, the wicked, not so') looks like a translator's or scribe's expansion that fills out the short Hebrew line. No Hebrew witness has it.

a: I myself have put my king in place
p: In the Greek the king speaks: 'I was set up as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and I, I have installed my king
readings.plain: I myself have put my king in place

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page)
readings.orig: ἐγὼ δὲ κατεστάθην βασιλεὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: but I was set up as king by him
readings.plain: I was set up as king by him

why: The Hebrew is the harder and older form: the LORD speaks in 2:6 and the king begins in 2:7. The Greek reads the same consonants as a passive and changes 'my holy mountain' to 'his holy mountain', so that the king's speech runs from 2:6 on; the Vulgate adds 'proclaiming his decree'.
b: If the Greek is chosen, the next words should also read 'on Zion, his holy mountain'.

a: You will crush them with an iron rod
p: The Greek reads 'you will shepherd them', and Revelation quotes that reading three times.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you will break them with a rod of iron
readings.plain: You will crush them with an iron rod

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Syriac; Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('reges eos', 'you will rule them')
readings.en: you will shepherd them with a rod of iron
readings.plain: You will shepherd them with an iron rod

why: The Hebrew consonants trʿm can be read as tero'em, 'you will break them' (from ra'a', the Aramaic-type form of 'break'), as the Masoretes did, or as tir'em, 'you will shepherd them' (from ra'ah). 'Break' matches the parallel 'shatter them like a jar'. The Greek reading is not a careless error: a king was a 'shepherd' with a rod (Micah 7:14), and Revelation 2:27, Revelation 12:5 and Revelation 19:15 follow it, picturing the Messiah's rule as both shepherding and smashing.

a: Kiss the son
p: The most debated words in Psalm 2. The witnesses read them four ways.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read as Aramaic bar, 'son'; Syriac; KJV, NIV, ESV
The same Hebrew, read as bar 'pure': Aquila and Symmachus (as reported), Jerome's Psalter iuxta Hebraeos ('adorate pure'); NJPS 'pay homage in good faith'

Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('apprehendite disciplinam'); the Targum ('receive instruction', as reported)
A modern conjecture joining 2:11b and 2:12a, reading beraglav ('his feet') for bar (NRSV)

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic consonants in their most common sense. Bar is the Aramaic word for 'son' (the Hebrew of 2:7 has ben); some argue that an Aramaic word was chosen on purpose for foreign kings, or to avoid the clash of sounds in nashshequ ben pen. Kissing was a sign of homage to a king (1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Kings 19:18). The other readings are serious: 'pure' is another meaning of Hebrew bar (24:4), the Greek and Targum seem to have read or interpreted a different word, and the conjecture removes the odd 'rejoice with trembling'. The Greek also says 'lest the Lord be angry' and 'perish from the righteous way'.
b: Christian readers since the fathers have heard the line of the Son of 2:7; Jewish interpreters differ: Rashi reads the line as a call to arm oneself with purity, while Ibn Ezra accepts 'son', meaning the king of 2:7. Jerome himself translated 'adore purely' in his Hebrew Psalter, while defending 'son' as a possible meaning in his Apology against Rufinus.

a: the LORD has picked out his loyal one
p: The Greek and Vulgate read 'the LORD has made his holy one wonderful'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: know that the LORD has set apart a loyal one for himself
readings.plain: the LORD has picked out his loyal one

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('mirificavit'); some Hebrew manuscripts reading hifli'
readings.en: the Lord has made his holy one wonderful
readings.plain: the LORD has made his loyal one wonderful

why: The two Hebrew verbs hiflah (set apart, distinguish) and hifli' (make wonderful) differ by one silent letter. Some scholars prefer 'has shown wonderful loyal love to me' (reading hifli' chasdo li, compare 17:7; 31:21). The Masoretic reading makes good sense and is kept.

a: their grain and new wine
p: The Greek adds 'and oil' to grain and new wine.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: their grain and their new wine

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('frumenti, vini et olei sui')
readings.orig: σίτου καὶ οἴνου καὶ ἐλαίου αὐτῶν
readings.en: of their grain and wine and oil
readings.plain: their grain, new wine and oil

why: Grain, new wine and oil are a fixed set of harvest blessings (Deuteronomy 7:13; Hosea 2:8), so a copyist or translator could easily complete the set. The shorter Hebrew is more likely to be original.

a: a God who shows his fury every day
p: The Greek says God is 'patient, not bringing on wrath every day'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and a God who is indignant every day
readings.plain: a God who shows his fury every day

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('fortis et patiens, numquid irascitur per singulos dies?')
readings.orig: καὶ ἰσχυρὸς καὶ μακρόθυμος μὴ ὀργὴν ἐπάγων καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν
readings.en: and strong and patient, not bringing on wrath every day
readings.plain: a God strong and patient, who does not bring on his fury every day

why: The Greek seems to read el, 'God', as al, 'not', and adds 'strong and patient' from the description of God in Exodus 34:6. The Hebrew line, God's daily indignation at evil, fits the threat of 7:12–13 and is kept.

a: you have founded a strong defense
p: The Greek has 'you have prepared praise', the words Jesus quotes in Matthew 21:16.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: you have founded a strong defense

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('perfecisti laudem'); Matthew 21:16

why: This is a difference of translation, not of Hebrew text: 'oz means 'strength', and in a few hymns 'strength' ascribed to God comes close to 'praise' (29:1; 96:7). The Plain English Translation gives the ordinary sense of the Hebrew and shows the Greek because the New Testament quotes it.

a: only a little less than God
p: The Greek, the Targum and Hebrews 2:7 read 'angels' for Hebrew elohim.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (elohim)

readings.plain: only a little less than God

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page); Targum and Syriac (as reported); Hebrews 2:7; KJV
readings.plain: only a little less than the angels

why: The Hebrew word is the usual word for God, and the echo of Genesis 1:26–27 favors 'God'. But elohim can mean heavenly beings, and the ancient translations all took it so. See the note at 8:5.

a: the afflicted
p: The written text and the reading tradition swap two similar words in 9:12, 9:18 and 10:12.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv) 'aniyyim; the Plain English Translation follows the Ketiv in all three places
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), reading tradition (Qere) 'anavim; KJV

why: 'Ani (afflicted, poor) and 'anav (humble, meek) differ by one letter that scribes often confused, and in the Psalms they overlap in meaning: the poor who depend on God. The Masoretes read 'humble' here and in 10:12, 'afflicted' in 9:18, the reverse of what is written each time. The Plain English Translation follows the written text in all three places.

a: the humble
p: Here the written text has 'humble' and the reading tradition 'afflicted'. See 9:12.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv) 'anavim
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), reading tradition (Qere) 'aniyyim; most English versions

why: As at 9:12 and 10:12, the Plain English Translation follows the written Hebrew. The sense is close either way.

a: Set fear over them, LORD.
p: The Greek reads 'Appoint a lawgiver over them, Lord'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (morah, 'fear')

Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('constitue legislatorem')
readings.en: appoint a lawgiver over them, Lord
readings.plain: Set a teacher of the law over them, LORD.

why: The Greek read the consonants mwrh as moreh, 'teacher', not mora', 'fear' (the Masoretic spelling is unusual, without the final alef). 'Fear' fits the parallel 'let the nations learn that they are mere mortals'. Some church fathers read the Greek 'lawgiver' as Christ or the Antichrist.

a: the afflicted
p: The written text has 'afflicted', the reading tradition 'humble'. See 9:12.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv) 'aniyyim
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), reading tradition (Qere) 'anavim; KJV

why: As at 9:12 and 9:18.

a: Fly off to your mountain, bird!
p: The written text says 'flee' to many; the reading tradition to one. The Greek has 'Move to the mountains like a sparrow'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), reading tradition (Qere) nudi, said to 'my soul' (feminine singular)
readings.plain: Fly off to your mountain, bird!

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv) nudu, plural
readings.en: flee, all of you, to your mountain, bird
readings.plain: Fly off, all of you, to your mountain like a bird!

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page); Syriac and Targum (as reported)
readings.orig: μεταναστεύου ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη ὡς στρουθίον
readings.en: move to the mountains like a sparrow
readings.plain: Fly off to the mountains like a sparrow!

why: The Qere fits 'my soul' in the same verse. The Greek and other versions read 'like a bird' (kemo tsippor), which may preserve an older text in which harkhem, 'your mountain', was 'mountain like'. The sense, 'run to the hills', is the same in every form.

a: he will rain down traps
p: Many scholars change one letter to read 'coals'. The Hebrew, Greek and Vulgate all have 'snares'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page) (pagidas); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('laqueos')
Symmachus (Greek translation of about AD 200, 'coals', as reported); a modern correction to pachame (NRSV, many commentaries)

why: All the main witnesses read 'snares', the harder reading. 'Coals' smooths the picture of a storm of fire but has little support. Raining traps may be a deliberate mixed image: judgment falls like rain and catches like a snare.

a: will keep them safe
p: The Hebrew has 'them' and then 'him'; the Greek and Vulgate have 'us' both times.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)

Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page); some Hebrew manuscripts (as reported)

why: The Hebrew 'them' points back to the afflicted and needy of 12:5, or to the LORD's words of 12:6 (Rashi, Ibn Ezra), and the singular 'him' in the next line to the one in need. The versions smoothed the persons to 'us'. The two halves of the verse go together; see the next entry.

a: you will protect him
p: Goes with the previous entry: Hebrew 'him', Greek 'us'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page)

why: The Hebrew form titsrennu can be read 'you will guard him' or, less usually, 'you will guard us'. The Plain English Translation takes the common sense.

a: for he has been generous to me.
p: The Greek and Vulgate end Psalm 13 with an extra line borrowed from 7:17.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for he has dealt fully with me
readings.plain: for he has been generous to me.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('et psallam nomini Domini altissimi')
readings.orig: τῷ εὐεργετήσαντί με καὶ ψαλῶ τῷ ὀνόματι κυρίου τοῦ ὑψίστου
readings.en: who has been good to me, and I will make music to the name of the Lord Most High
readings.plain: for he has been generous to me. / I will make music to the name of the LORD Most High.

why: The extra line is word for word the end of 7:17, and probably came in from there. The Hebrew is shorter and is kept. In Hebrew Bibles, English 13:5–6 is one verse, 13:6.

a: No one does good, no, not a single one.
p: Many Greek and Latin copies add six lines here. They are the lines Paul quotes in Romans 3:13–18.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Psalm 53:3; some Greek manuscripts (as reported)
readings.en: no one does good, not even one
readings.plain: No one does good, no, not a single one.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page) (printed in the Greek text on the sacred-texts.com page; found in Codex Vaticanus and other copies, as reported); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page); the Coverdale Psalter in the Book of Common Prayer
readings.orig: τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος ὁ λάρυγξ αὐτῶν ... οὐκ ἔστιν φόβος θεοῦ ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν
readings.en: their throat is an open grave ... there is no fear of God before their eyes
readings.plain: No one does good, no, not a single one. / Their throat is a grave left open; / with their tongues they deceive. / The poison of snakes is under their lips. / Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; / their feet are quick to shed blood. / Ruin and misery are on their roads, / and the road of peace they have not known. / There is no fear of God before their eyes.

why: The added lines are exactly the series Paul quotes in Romans 3:13–18 from Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7, Isaiah 59:7–8 and Psalm 36:1. Almost all scholars think Christian scribes copied them from Romans into the Greek psalm, though a few have argued that Paul found them already joined. Jerome noted the problem and that the lines are not in the Hebrew. They are in no Hebrew witness and not in Psalm 53, so the Plain English Translation leaves them out.
b: The lines reached English through the Latin: the Coverdale Psalter of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer, still sung in Anglican churches, includes them as Psalm 14:5–7 in its own numbering.

a: He swears to his own cost
t: To his harm or to his neighbor?
p: The Greek read 'he swears to his neighbor and does not break it'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: he swears to do harm (to himself)
readings.plain: He swears to his own cost

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('qui iurat proximo suo')

why: The Greek read the consonants lhr' as le-rea', 'to the neighbor' (with the Hebrew h taken as part of the article or ignored). The Masoretic 'to (his) harm' is the harder reading and makes the point sharper: he keeps his word even when it costs him.

a: I said to the LORD
p: The Hebrew has 'you (feminine) said'; the Greek, Syriac and Jerome have 'I said'. The Plain English Translation follows 'I said', a choice between ancient witnesses.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page); Jerome iuxta Hebraeos; the Syriac and some Hebrew manuscripts (as reported)
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), 'amart (feminine 'you said'); the Targum ('you said, my soul', as reported); Rashi; KJV 'O my soul, thou hast said'

why: The Greek, the Syriac and Jerome read 'I said', and so do some Hebrew manuscripts (as reported). The Targum and the medieval Jewish commentators keep 'you said', addressed to the speaker's own soul, as the KJV also supplies. The Plain English Translation follows 'I said' because the rest of the psalm speaks in the first person and the Masoretic amart may be an old spelling of amarti, 'I said', without its final letter. The witnesses are divided, so this is a choice, not a unanimous reading. It is one of the few places where the Plain English Translation departs from the Masoretic Text in this part.

a: Many pains await those who rush after another god.
p: The Greek reads 'their weaknesses were multiplied; afterward they hurried', which changes how 16:3–4 reads.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: their pains will multiply, (those who) hurry after another
readings.plain: Many pains await those who rush after another god.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('multiplicatae sunt infirmitates eorum, postea acceleraverunt')
readings.orig: ἐπληθύνθησαν αἱ ἀσθένειαι αὐτῶν, μετὰ ταῦτα ἐτάχυναν
readings.en: their weaknesses were multiplied; afterward they hurried
readings.plain: Their weaknesses grew many; afterward they hurried.

why: The Greek read the same consonants with different sense: acher, 'another', as achar, 'afterward', and the 'pains' as weaknesses. It then reads 16:3–4 as about the holy ones: their weaknesses grew many, and afterward they hurried. The Hebrew sets those who run after other gods against the psalmist, which fits 16:4b, where he will not pour their drink offerings. See the note on 16:3.

a: my honor celebrates
p: The Greek has 'my tongue', the reading quoted in Acts 2:26.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)

Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('exultavit lingua mea'); Acts 2:26

why: The Hebrew 'my glory' stands for the whole self, as in 30:12 and 57:8. The Greek is a free rendering, perhaps thinking of the tongue as the organ of praise. It is a difference of translation more than of text.

a: settle down in safety
p: The Greek has 'will dwell in hope', the wording of Acts 2:26.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)

Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('requiescet in spe'); Acts 2:26

why: Lavetach means 'in safety, securely'. The Greek translators often rendered words from this root as 'hope', which Acts 2:26 reads as hope of resurrection. Goes with the previous entry.

a: to see the Pit
p: The Greek has 'to see corruption', the wording on which Acts 2:27–31 and Acts 13:35–37 build.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)

Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('videre corruptionem'); Acts 2:27; Acts 13:35

why: The Hebrew noun shachat means 'pit, grave' and is parallel to Sheol in the first line. The Greek connected it with the verb 'to destroy, corrupt'. The two readings are close in effect: not to see the grave is not to suffer the decay of death. See the note.

a: your loyal one
p: The Leningrad Codex writes the singular. Many other manuscripts and printed editions write a plural spelling, read aloud as the singular.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written and read as singular; Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page) (ton hosion sou); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page); Acts 2:27; Acts 13:35
Many medieval Hebrew manuscripts and printed Rabbinic Bibles, written (Ketiv) with yod as a plural, with the singular as the reading tradition (Qere) (as reported)

why: The Leningrad Codex has the singular with no marginal note. In much of the Masoretic tradition the plural spelling is the written text (Ketiv) and the singular is what is read (Qere); the plural spelling may also be an old way of writing the singular with its suffix. The singular matches 'my life' in the first line and has all the ancient versions. Medieval Jewish writers sometimes pointed to the plural spelling against the Christian reading of the verse as one person (as reported); the New Testament argument (Acts 2:27; Acts 13:35–37) rests on the singular, which the reading tradition also keeps.

a: Now they have hemmed in our steps on every side
p: The written text has 'surrounded me', the reading tradition 'surrounded us'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), reading tradition (Qere) sevavunu, 'us'
readings.en: our steps: now they have surrounded us
readings.plain: Now they have hemmed in our steps on every side

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv) sevavuni, 'me'; Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page) ('they surrounded me')
readings.en: our steps: now they have surrounded me
readings.plain: Our steps they track, and now they have hemmed me in on every side

why: The Qere matches 'our steps' and 'us' later in the verse. The Greek, 'casting me out, now they have surrounded me', supports the written 'me'. The psalm moves between 'I' and 'we' elsewhere too.

a: When I wake up, I will be filled with the sight of your form.
p: The Greek reads 'I will be satisfied when your glory appears'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: I will be satisfied, when awaking, with your form
readings.plain: When I wake up, I will be filled with the sight of your form.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 200s–100s BC; Rahlfs, checked on the sacred-texts.com polyglot page); Vulgate, Gallican Psalter (Jerome's revision from the Greek; checked on the same page) ('satiabor cum apparuerit gloria tua')
readings.orig: χορτασθήσομαι ἐν τῷ ὀφθῆναι τὴν δόξαν σου
readings.en: I will be satisfied when your glory is seen
readings.plain: I will be filled when your glory appears.

why: The Greek seems to have avoided saying that a human sees God's 'form', and may have read be-hera'ot, 'when it appears', for be-haqits, 'when awaking'. The Hebrew is kept.
